newsitem.title: UK: MOTOR RACING-HILL SAVOURS LIFE AT THE TOP.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-HILL SAVOURS LIFE AT THE TOP.

text.p: High above the streets where he once weaved between peak-hour traffic as a motorbike dispatch rider, Damon Hill savoured life at the top.
"I'm still flying," Hill reflected on Wednesday, four days after clinching the Formula One world drivers' title in Suzuka, Japan.
"I have not yet come down from this. I think it is going to rebound but it will take a few weeks yet."
In the third floor restaurant of a leading London department store, bedecked with miniature Union Jacks, Hill recalled the days when he dreamt of making his name as a motor cycle racer.

"I always had the intention of getting off bikes even though I loved it. I didn't plan to be a dispatch driver all my life," Hill said. "It was all part of my plan in order for me to get money to go racing."
Hill was given a motor bike at the age of 11 by his father Graham, world champion in 1962 and 1968, who died in a light aircraft crash in 1975.
A privileged childhood with a father he loved came to a shattering end as insurance claims left the Hill family close to penury.
Hill turned to bikes and the nascent punk rock movement, playing in a band named Sex Hitler and the Hormones in the calculated bad taste of the era.
Despite initial successes on the bike circuit, the lure of the four wheel circuits became irresistible after Hill's mother paid for a week's driving course in Magny-Cours, France in 1984.
Graduating through Formula Ford, British Formula Three and and the international F3000 championship, Hill became a test driver for Williams in 1991.
He retained the job in the following year, when he also raced in Formula one for the Brabham team. In 1993 he was given the number two post to Alain Prost, finishing third in the title race.
The comparisons with his father had now started, providing irresistible copy for newspaper colummnists spinning tales of a son driven to prove himself a champion in his own right.
"I don't know where the idea came from," Hill said. "I'm not in competition with my father.
"I simply adored him, I don't want to take anything away from him. He died 21 years ago, that was an awfully long time ago and I've long since handled that emotion."
Hill remained the impeccable diplomat when asked about the Williams's team decision to drop him at the end of the season.
"It wasn't quite the pat on the back I had been expecting," he said. "I have got used to it now. Every season there's some sort of drama that crops up.
"But I really had the ropes pulled out from me there."
After rest, reflection and a holiday with his wife Georgia and their three children, Hill will concentrate on his new role in the Arrows team.
"I am not going to sit here and say I'll defend my championship next year, that would be stretching it," he said.
"But I certainly think we will surprise a few people. I think we will have success on our own terms.
"We will have a target to go for and a goal and, although I'm not saying that sixth in a race will be good enough for me, you always set targets as high as you can get until you get to the front.
"I would like to see progression and for us to get better throughout the season and build towards future seasons.
